estimate.normalised_text: A margin of error tells you how precise a Census Bureau ACS estimate is: the Bureau publishes MOEs at a 90 percent confidence level, so adding and subtracting the MOE from an estimate gives a range that should contain the true population value 90 percent of the time — for example, Colorado's 2015 estimate of 564,757 one-person households (MOE 10,127) means the real number was likely between 554,630 and 574,884. Related measures derived from the MOE, the standard error and the coefficient of variation, indicate how much sampling error an estimate carries, with smaller values signaling a more reliable estimate.

estimate.normalised_text: Census data comes with a margin of error, so to check whether two estimates really differ, you convert each margin of error into a standard error (divide by 1.645) and combine them into a test value — if that value exceeds 1.645, the gap is statistically significant at the 90 percent confidence level. Using 2015 ACS data on householders 65 and older who live alone, Florida (12.6 percent) tested well above Arizona (10.5 percent) with a value of 9.581, a real difference, while Indiana (10.8 percent) versus Arizona gave only 1.369, a gap small enough that it could be due to chance.

Because both inputs carry some sampling error, the derived figure comes with its own margin of error (about ±202,000, or a 90 percent confidence range of roughly 61.19 to 61.60 million) — a spread small enough, at about 0.2 percent of the estimate, to call the result highly reliable.

The Census Bureau's example adds up the number of never-married women in Fairfax County, Arlington County, and Alexandria City, Virginia, from the 2015 ACS to get a combined total of 203,119 — with a margin of error of about ±5,070, found by squaring each county's margin of error, adding them, and taking the square root.

Because that margin is tiny compared with the estimate itself, the combined figure is considered very reliable.

## What this data is

These are U.S. Census Bureau figures (table B19013) showing median household income for Colorado counties — the income of the household right in the middle, where half of the county's households earn more and half earn less. It's a better measure of a "typical" household than an average, since a handful of very wealthy households can pull an average upward.

Each county has two numbers: the estimate itself, and a margin of error. These figures come from a survey of a sample of households, not a count of everyone, so the true value sits somewhere in a range around the estimate.

## What it says

The list is alphabetical and stops at "B" — these are 7 of Colorado's 64 counties.

County: Typical household income; Give or take.
Boulder: Typical household income: $102,772; Give or take: ±$2,628.
Arapahoe: Typical household income: $97,215; Give or take: ±$1,592.
Adams: Typical household income: $91,387; Give or take: ±$1,470.
Archuleta: Typical household income: $76,524; Give or take: ±$6,714.
Alamosa: Typical household income: $51,445; Give or take: ±$6,098.
Bent: Typical household income: $49,194; Give or take: ±$4,596.
Baca: Typical household income: $40,380; Give or take: ±$7,753.

The headline: a typical household in Boulder County earns roughly two and a half times what a typical household in Baca County earns — about $103,000 versus about $40,000.

The pattern: the three highest-income counties here (Boulder, Arapahoe, Adams) are all in the Denver metro area. The lower-income ones (Baca, Bent, Alamosa) are rural counties in southern and southeastern Colorado.

A caution about precision: the margins of error are much larger for the small rural counties, because fewer households there were surveyed. Baca County's figure could plausibly be anywhere from about $33,000 to $48,000 — a range that overlaps with Bent County's and Alamosa's. So while it's safe to say those three counties are all substantially poorer than the Denver-area ones, ranking them against each other isn't supported by this data. The Denver-area figures, by contrast, are precise enough (±2–3%) that their ordering is meaningful.

We drop a table from publication when most of its estimates are too shaky to trust — specifically, when over half the numbers at the most detailed level have a margin of error so wide that the estimate can't be told apart from zero (a coefficient of variation above 0.61, roughly the 90 percent confidence threshold).

This rule applies to both the base and collapsed detailed tables, and estimates of zero — which have no meaningful error measure — are counted as unreliable when we check whether the table clears the bar.

estimate.normalised_text:
Jobs report in plain language

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics said today that July was a quiet month for the job market. Total employment outside of farming fell by 23,000 — a small change by the standards of a job market this size — and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent.

The declines were concentrated in two areas: local government education (public school jobs) and retail stores. Health care, meanwhile, kept adding jobs, continuing a run it's been on for a while.

Why "changed little" for a 23,000 drop

These numbers come from a survey of employers, not a count of every job in the country, so they carry a margin of error. For the monthly change in total employment, that margin is about plus or minus 122,000 jobs.

So a reported change of 23,000, in either direction, is well inside the noise. It's too small to tell us confidently whether hiring actually went up or down.

## Health in Newfoundland and Labrador, 2022

This is Statistics Canada survey data for Newfoundland and Labrador in 2022, covering people 12 and older, both sexes combined. Four findings:

Adult obesity — about 42%. Among adults 18 and over, 41.9% were classified as obese based on their self-reported height and weight (adjusted to correct for the well-known tendency to under-report weight). The survey's margin of error puts the true figure somewhere between 38.9% and 44.9%.

Youth overweight or obesity — about 38%. Among youth aged 12 to 17, 37.5% were overweight or obese. This number is flagged "use with caution" — the sample was small enough that the plausible range is very wide, from 26.4% to 50.1%. Treat it as a rough signal, not a precise measurement.

Arthritis — about 27%. Just over a quarter of people 15 and older (27.3%) reported having arthritis, with a plausible range of 25.3% to 29.4%.

Diabetes — about 12%. Roughly one in eight people (12.4%) reported having diabetes, plausible range 10.6% to 14.5%.

### How to read the ranges

Every percentage comes with a "95% confidence interval" — a low and high bound. Because these figures come from a sample rather than a headcount of every resident, the interval says: if the survey were repeated many times, the true population value would fall inside this range 95% of the time. Narrow ranges (arthritis, diabetes) mean a well-measured estimate; wide ones (youth weight) mean the estimate is shaky.

Statistics Canada also attaches quality flags to values. The only one appearing here is E — "use with caution," on the youth figures. Other flags in their system mark data that is suppressed for privacy, too unreliable to publish, preliminary, or revised.

### One caveat worth noting

The height and weight figures are self-reported, not measured by a clinician. The adult numbers have been statistically adjusted to compensate for this; the youth numbers have not, so they may understate the actual rate.

Health indicators for Prince Edward Island, 2022 (Statistics Canada, both sexes, based on a survey of people 12 and over)

Obesity in adults (18+): About 36% of PEI adults were classified as obese based on their own reported height and weight, adjusted to correct for the tendency people have to under-report weight. Because this comes from a sample rather than everyone in the province, the true figure is most likely somewhere between 30% and 43% — roughly one in three adults.

Overweight or obesity in youth (12–17): About 32% of PEI teens fell into the overweight-or-obese range, with a likely true range of 21% to 45%. Statistics Canada flags this number with an "E," meaning use it with caution — the sample was small enough that the estimate is shaky. The wide range says the same thing: it could be as low as one in five teens or as high as nearly one in two.

Arthritis (15+): About 19% of Islanders 15 and over reported having arthritis, likely between 15% and 23% — close to one in five.

Diabetes: About 9% reported having diabetes, likely between 6% and 13% — roughly one in eleven.

A note on reading these numbers. Every figure is an estimate from a survey, not a count. The "confidence interval" is the range the real value very probably falls in (19 times out of 20); a wide range means less certainty, usually because fewer people in that group were surveyed. The height and weight figures are also self-reported, which people are known to shade in flattering directions — the adult numbers have been statistically adjusted for that, the youth numbers have not.

## Alberta's job market, July 2026

(Statistics Canada Labour Force Survey, seasonally adjusted. All figures come from a monthly sample survey, so each one carries a margin of error.)

The basics

Alberta had about 4.15 million people aged 15 and over. Of those:

- 2.87 million were in the labour force — meaning they either had a job or were actively looking for one.
- 2.67 million were working: 2.20 million full-time and 467,000 part-time.
- 202,000 were unemployed — without work but looking for it.
- The remaining ~1.28 million were outside the labour force entirely: retirees, students, people caring for family, people not currently job-hunting.

The three headline rates

Rate: Value; What it means.
Unemployment rate: 7.0%; Of everyone who wanted a job, 7 in 100 couldn't find one.
Participation rate: 69.2%; About 7 in 10 adults were working or job-hunting.
Employment rate: 64.3%; About 64 in 100 adults actually had a job.

A note on precision. These are survey estimates, not a headcount, and the file reports the uncertainty alongside each number. The unemployment rate's standard error is 0.4 points, so the true figure is roughly 7.0% ± 0.8 at conventional (95%) confidence — somewhere in the low-6s to high-7s. The employment figure of 2,670,000 carries a standard error of about 19,800, so it's good to within roughly ±40,000. Month-to-month wiggles smaller than that aren't real news.

"Seasonally adjusted" means the numbers have been smoothed to remove predictable annual patterns — summer student hiring, holiday retail, construction slowdowns in winter — so this month can be compared fairly against any other month.

One caveat on scope: this is the all-genders, all-ages-15-and-over total. The file doesn't break the numbers out by gender or age group, so it can't say whether, for example, youth unemployment differs from the 7.0% overall figure.

estimate.normalised_text: Before the current standards, NCHS used two different rules of thumb for deciding when a rate was too shaky to publish: vital statistics rates (births and deaths) were suppressed if fewer than 20 events were counted — roughly a 23% relative standard error — while health care survey rates followed a "30/30 rule," suppressed below 30 sample observations and flagged as unreliable above a 30% relative standard error. When a rate's denominator came from a survey like the Census Bureau's ACS or CPS rather than a census count, the extra sampling error had to be factored in, and rates with a relative standard error at or above 23% were suppressed or sent for internal review.

estimate.normalised_text:
Dental visits among older adults, 2022

In 2022, about 2 out of 3 adults age 65 and older (63.7%) saw a dentist at some point during the previous year.

- Men and women: Women were slightly more likely than men to have gone — 64.9% of women compared with 62.3% of men.
- Age: Dental visits became less common with age. About 65.4% of people ages 65–74 and 63.6% of those ages 75–84 had seen a dentist in the past year, but that fell to 53.3% among those age 85 and older — roughly half.

Source: Figure 1 and Table 1, United States, 2022. Percentages are survey estimates; each carries a margin of error (for example, the total of 63.7% ranges from 62.4% to 65.1%), and the estimate for adults 85 and older is the least precise because it is based on a smaller group.

Figure 4 data: Perinatal deaths by state, 2022 vs. 2023

The perinatal mortality rate counts babies who die shortly before or shortly after birth. It's expressed as deaths per 1,000 births — so a rate of 9.44 means about 9 such deaths for every 1,000 births.

This table shows the rate for each state in 2022 and again in 2023, and whether the change between those two years was large enough to be a real shift rather than ordinary year-to-year fluctuation. A dagger (†) marks changes that were not statistically meaningful — the numbers moved, but not by enough to conclude anything changed. Where a percentage appears instead, the change was real.

For the states shown in this excerpt:

State: 2022; 2023; What changed.
Alabama: 9.44; 10.96; Rose 16% — a real increase.
Alaska: 8.39; 7.73; Drop not meaningful.
Arizona: 9.56; 9.28; Drop not meaningful.
Arkansas: 10.86; 11.49; Rise not meaningful.
California: 7.30; 7.25; Essentially unchanged.
Colorado: 7.32; 8.61; Rose 18% — a real increase.
Connecticut: 6.93; 7.63; Rise not meaningful.
Delaware: 9.66; 8.68; Drop not meaningful.

The takeaway: Among these states, only Alabama and Colorado saw increases big enough to count as genuine change — up 16% and 18%, respectively. Everywhere else, the year-to-year movement falls within normal statistical noise. Rates in this group ranged from under 7 per 1,000 (Connecticut, California) to over 11 (Arkansas).

Two notes on the source: the full figure covers all 50 states and the District of Columbia, but the text you provided stops at Delaware — so this is an alphabetical excerpt, not the complete picture. And "statistically significant" here uses the standard p = 0.05 threshold, meaning a change is only flagged as real if there's less than a 1-in-20 chance it's a fluke.

estimate.normalised_text:
## Understanding Margin of Error in ACS Data — Plain Language Version

What a margin of error tells you

The American Community Survey (ACS) asks a sample of people questions rather than counting everyone, so its numbers are estimates, not exact counts. The margin of error (MOE) tells you how close that estimate probably is to the real number for the whole population.

The Census Bureau publishes MOEs at a 90 percent confidence level. Add and subtract the MOE from the estimate, and you get a range — the confidence interval — that should contain the true value about 90 percent of the time.

A worked example

The 2015 ACS 1-year estimates say Colorado had 564,757 one-person households, with an MOE of 10,127.

- Lower bound: 564,757 − 10,127 = 554,630
- Upper bound: 564,757 + 10,127 = 574,884

So we can be 90 percent confident the true number falls between roughly 554,600 and 574,900. Put another way: if the survey were repeated 100 times, about 90 of those estimates would land inside that range.

The smaller the MOE compared to the estimate itself, the narrower the range — and the more precise the estimate.

A caution about the edges of the range

Confidence intervals can produce results that don't make sense in the real world. If an estimate is close to zero, subtracting the MOE may give a negative number — but there's no such thing as a negative number of people, so report the lower bound as zero. Similarly, a percentage can't exceed 100 percent. (Some measures, like income, can legitimately be negative.) Always sanity-check the range against what the number actually represents.

Two related measures

Standard error (SE) measures how much an estimate is likely to bounce around simply because it came from a sample. It's the building block behind the MOE, and you get it by dividing the MOE by 1.645. For the Colorado example: 10,127 ÷ 1.645 ≈ 6,156.

Standard error depends on how varied the population is and how big the sample is. Bigger samples mean smaller standard errors — which is exactly why the Census Bureau publishes estimates for small places only by pooling several years of data together. More years means more sample, which means more reliable numbers.

Coefficient of variation (CV) expresses the standard error as a percentage of the estimate itself, which makes it easy to compare reliability across very different numbers. For Colorado: 6,156 ÷ 564,757 ≈ 1.1 percent
Colorado: Coefficient of variation of 1.1 percent..

A small CV means the sampling error is small relative to the estimate — the number is reliable. A large CV means the error is nearly as big as the estimate itself, and the number should be treated with caution. Because CVs are percentages, most people find them easier to compare across a set of estimates than raw standard errors.

A large CV means the error is nearly as big as the estimate itself, and the number should be treated with caution. Plain-language version

Suppose you want to know whether two survey estimates are really different, or whether the gap between them is just noise from sampling. Here's how that check works, using 2015 American Community Survey data on the share of householders age 65 or older who live alone.

The estimates

- Florida: 12.6 percent, margin of error ±0.2
- Arizona: 10.5 percent, margin of error ±0.3
- Indiana: 10.8 percent, margin of error ±0.2

Step 1 — Convert each margin of error into a standard error. Divide the margin of error by 1.645. Florida's becomes 0.122, Arizona's becomes 0.182, and Indiana's becomes 0.122. (The standard error is just a measure of how much an estimate would bounce around if the survey were repeated.)

Step 2 — Compare the gap to the noise. Take the difference between the two estimates and divide it by the combined standard error of the pair. That gives a "test value" — essentially, how many units of survey noise the gap is worth.

Step 3 — Compare the test value to 1.645. That's the cutoff for 90 percent confidence.

Florida vs. Arizona: The gap is 2.1 percentage points, and the test value comes out to 9.581. That's far above 1.645, so the difference is statistically significant at the 90 percent confidence level. Roughly speaking: you can be 90 percent confident that Florida and Arizona genuinely differ on this measure.

Indiana vs. Arizona: The gap is only 0.3 percentage points, and the test value is 1.369 — below the 1.645 cutoff. The difference is not statistically significant. Roughly speaking: the observed gap is small enough that it could easily be a product of chance, and the data don't let you conclude the two states actually differ.

The takeaway: A visible difference between two estimates isn't automatically a real difference. Whether it counts depends on both how big the gap is and how precise the underlying estimates are. A 2.1-point gap between precisely measured estimates is convincing; a 0.3-point gap is not.

General-audience restatement

Census data on data.census.gov includes a table (Demographic Profile DP03) that already groups household incomes into broad categories. That gives us a useful test: we can compare the shortcut method for combining margins of error — the approximation shown earlier — against the Census Bureau's own published figures, which are calculated directly and account for the fact that errors in the individual income groups are related to one another (their covariance).

The comparison uses Loudoun County, Virginia, from the 2015 ACS 1-year estimates:

Income category: Subgroup; Households; Margin of error; Standard error; Coefficient of variation.
$15,000–$24,999: Subgroup: 1; Households: 3,497; Margin of error: ±1,037; Standard error: 630; Coefficient of variation: 18.0%.
$25,000–$34,999: Subgroup: 2; Households: 3,537; Margin of error: ±973; Standard error: 591; Coefficient of variation: 16.7%.
$35,000–$49,999: Subgroup: 3; Households: 7,270; Margin of error: ±1,554; Standard error: 945; Coefficient of variation: 13.0%.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, data.census.gov, Table DP03, "Selected Economic Characteristics."

What the comparison shows: For Subgroups 1 and 3, the shortcut method produces margins of error, standard errors, and coefficients of variation that are essentially the same as the published values. Subgroup 2 is the exception. There, the shortcut gives a margin of error of ±931, while the published value is ±973 — the shortcut understates the uncertainty. The same gap appears in the coefficient of variation: 16.0 percent by the shortcut versus 16.7 percent using the published margin of error.

The takeaway: The approximation is usually close, but it can make an estimate look slightly more precise than it really is. When published figures are available, use them.

## Combining a count with a percentage — in plain language

Sometimes the number you want isn't published directly, but you can build it from two numbers that are: a total count and a percentage of that total.

The example. Say you want to know how many owner-occupied homes in the U.S. are single-family detached houses. Two published figures from 2015 get you there:

- Owner-occupied housing units: 74,506,512, give or take 228,238
- Share that are 1-unit detached: 82.4%, give or take 0.1 percentage point

Multiply them: 74,506,512 × 0.824 ≈ 61,393,366 single-family detached owner-occupied homes.

The catch. Both inputs are survey estimates, not exact counts, so each carries a margin of error — a "give or take" range. When you multiply them, that uncertainty carries into the answer, and you have to combine the two margins rather than ignore them or simply add them. A standard formula (formula 9 in the source) does this; here it works out to a margin of error of 202,289.

Reading the result. The margin of error defines a 90 percent confidence interval — the range the true value very likely falls within. Add and subtract it:

> 61,393,366 ± 202,289 → 61,191,077 to 61,595,655

Is the estimate any good? Two quick checks:

- The standard error (202,289 ÷ 1.645) is about 122,972 — the underlying measure of sampling variability that the margin of error is built from.

## Adding Up Survey Estimates: A Worked Example

The question: How many never-married women live in the three Virginia communities that border Washington, DC — Fairfax County, Arlington County, and Alexandria City?

Because the American Community Survey (ACS) is a sample survey rather than a full count, every number it publishes is an estimate that comes with a stated range of uncertainty. That range is the margin of error (MOE). Here are the 2015 ACS 1-year figures:

Area: Estimate; Margin of error.
Fairfax County: Estimate: 135,173; Margin of error: ±3,860.
Arlington County: Estimate: 43,104; Margin of error: ±2,642.
Alexandria City: Estimate: 24,842; Margin of error: ±1,957.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, data.census.gov, Table B12001, "Sex by Marital Status for the Population 15 Years and Over."

### Step 1: Add the estimates

135,173 + 43,104 + 24,842 = 203,119

### Step 2: Combine the margins of error

Margins of error do not simply add up. If you added them (3,860 + 2,642 + 1,957 = 8,459), you would badly overstate the uncertainty, because the three areas' errors are independent and tend to partially cancel each other out. Instead, square each one, add the squares, and take the square root:

√(3,8602 + 2,6422 + 1,9572) = √25,709,613 ≈ ±5,070
Margins of error of 5,070.

So the combined estimate is 203,119 ± 5,070 never-married women.

### Step 3: Convert to standard errors (optional)

The MOE is just a rescaled standard error (SE) — the ACS uses a 90 percent confidence level, so MOE = 1.645 × SE. Divide by 1.645 to go the other direction:

- Fairfax: 3,860 ÷ 1.645 = 2,347
- Arlington: 2,642 ÷ 1.645 = 1,606
- Alexandria: 1,957 ÷ 1.645 = 1,190

Fairfax: SE of 2,347.
Arlington: SE of 1,606.
Alexandria: SE of 1,190.

Combine them the same way — square, sum, square root:

√(2,3472 + 1,6062 + 1,1902) ≈ 3,083

(Equivalently, 5,070 ÷ 1.645 ≈ 3,083.)

### Step 4: Judge how reliable the result is

A convenient reliability yardstick is the coefficient of variation (CV) — the standard error expressed as a percentage of the estimate:

CV ≈ 1.5 percent
coefficient of variation of 1.5 percent.

### What this means

A CV of about 1.5 percent means the sampling error is very small relative to the size of the estimate. In plain terms: the survey's uncertainty amounts to roughly a percent and a half of the number itself. The figure of about 203,000 never-married women in the Virginia communities bordering Washington, DC, is a highly reliable estimate, and users can cite it with confidence.

A CV of about 1.5 percent means the sampling error is very small relative to the size of the estimate. Every estimate in a table comes with a margin of error. We measure how shaky an estimate is using its coefficient of variation (CV) — basically, the size of the error compared to the size of the estimate itself. A bigger CV means a less trustworthy number.

We use a cutoff of 0.61. That value isn't arbitrary: an estimate with a CV above 0.61 is so imprecise that we can't confidently say it's different from zero at all (using a 90 percent confidence standard).

To decide about a whole table, we look at its typical estimate — the median CV, meaning the midpoint when all the estimates are ranked from most to least reliable. If that midpoint is above 0.61, it means more than half the numbers in the table fall into the "can't distinguish from zero" range, so we drop the table entirely.

Two details:

- Estimates of zero have no defined CV (you can't compare an error to nothing), so we treat them as 0.61's worst case — a CV of 1.0 — when finding the midpoint.
- Only the most detailed rows count. Tables often show subtotals and grand totals built from finer categories; including those would double-count, so we base the calculation only on the bottom-level lines.

## How the 2020 Census Protected Privacy in the Redistricting Data

When the Census Bureau released the P.L. 94-171 redistricting files in 2021, it protected people's confidentiality by adding carefully calibrated statistical noise to the published counts. The amount of noise is governed by a "privacy-loss budget" — a fixed quantity of allowable privacy loss that the Bureau divides up across the statistics it publishes. There, the estimate is judged reliable on absolute width alone — the relative-width (≤130%) test is never applied, because that test is scoped only to widths between 0.05 and 0.30.

Two conditions still gate presentation in that branch, but neither is a width test:
- number of events > 0 (an estimate of 0, or its complement 1, goes to the clearance official for statistical review), and
- the degrees-of-freedom criterion is met (failure likewise routes to statistical review, not automatic suppression).

Minimum denominator sample size = 30, and it is a hard suppression gate — not a reviewable one.

Publication status by case:

Condition: Status.
Denominator sample size < 30 (or effective denominator < 30, for complex surveys): Suppress. No review, no flag..
Denominator ≥ 30 (and effective denominator ≥ 30 where applicable): Gate passed — but not publishable yet. The estimate still has to clear the Clopper-Pearson / Korn-Graubard CI width criteria and the degrees-of-freedom criterion..

estimate.normalised_text:
Understanding the numbers behind employment estimates

Employment figures are based on a survey, not a count of every worker. Because a survey only reaches a sample of people, its results come with a margin of uncertainty. Statisticians measure that uncertainty with a number called the standard error, and use it to build a range — a "confidence interval" — around the reported figure.

An example

Suppose the reported change in total employment from one month to the next was an increase of 60,000, with a standard error of 25,000.

- Adding and subtracting one standard error gives a range of 35,000 to 85,000. There's roughly a 2-in-3 chance (68%) that this range contains the true change.
- Adding and subtracting two standard errors gives a range of 10,000 to 110,000. There's roughly a 19-in-20 chance (95%) that this range contains the true change.

Deciding whether a change is real

The point of these ranges is to answer a practical question: did employment actually change, or does the number just reflect the luck of which people happened to be surveyed?

The rule of thumb is simple. Look at the 95% range:

- If the range does not include zero, the change is treated as real — statisticians call it "statistically significant." In the example above, the range runs from 10,000 to 110,000, which is entirely above zero, so the 60,000 increase counts as a genuine change.
- If the range does include zero, the apparent change may well be noise from sampling, and shouldn't be read as real movement.

In general, the bigger a reported change is compared with its standard error, the more confident we can be that something actually happened. And when we say a result is significant "at the 5% level," we mean there's about a 5% risk of calling a change real when nothing actually changed.

Area: Minimum estimate that can be published.
Canada: 1,500 people.
Quebec, Ontario, Alberta, British Columbia: 1,500 each.
Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Manitoba, Saskatchewan: 500 each.

Yukon: 200.

estimate.normalised_text:
How Statistics Canada rates the reliability of survey estimates

When Statistics Canada publishes a number from a household survey, that number is an estimate based on a sample, not a count of everyone. The coefficient of variation (CV) measures how shaky that estimate is — roughly, how much it would bounce around if the survey were repeated. A low CV means a solid number; a high CV means a wobbly one.

Estimates fall into three buckets:

Category: CV; What it means.
1: CV: 16.5% or less; Publish freely. Reliable enough to use as-is, with no warning label..
2: CV: Over 16.5%, up to 33.3%; Publish with a caution. Still useful for some purposes, but readers must be told the estimate is uncertain..
3: CV: Over 33.3%; Don't publish. So imprecise it's likely to mislead..

For Category 3, there's a narrow exception. If someone asks for the data in a custom (non-standard) product and still wants it after being warned how unreliable it is, Statistics Canada may provide it — but only attached to a disclaimer. The person receiving it has to acknowledge the warning and agree never to share, present, or report the figures, directly or indirectly, without that disclaimer traveling with them.

Plain-language version

Survey numbers are estimates, not exact counts, so each one carries a margin of error. Statisticians express that error as a coefficient of variation (CV) — the size of the likely error stated as a percentage of the estimate itself. A smaller CV means a more reliable number.

Take Newfoundland and Labrador in January 2024. The survey estimated 28,000 people unemployed and 275,900 people in the labour force (everyone working or looking for work). Dividing one by the other gives an unemployment rate of 10.4%.

But both of those underlying figures are estimates with their own uncertainty. Table 7.1 shows the count of unemployed people has a CV of 5.0%, and the labour force count has a CV of 2.5%. Because the rate is built from both, its uncertainty draws on both.

A quick way to gauge the rate's reliability is simply to add the two CVs together: 5.0% + 2.5% = 7.5%. So the 10.4% unemployment rate carries an approximate CV of 7.5%.

This addition is a deliberately cautious shortcut — it assumes the two errors compound in the worst possible way, so the true uncertainty is generally somewhat smaller. It's used because it's easy to calculate and errs on the side of overstating, rather than understating, how uncertain the figure is.

One note on the source figures: 28,000 divided by 275,900 works out to 10.1%, not the 10.4% quoted. The published rate is calculated from unrounded data, so the small gap is a rounding artifact rather than an error in the example.

## What the table shows

This is a worked example from NCHS (National Center for Health Statistics), using 2013–2014 NHANES data on children aged 8–17. Its real subject isn't blood pressure — it's when a survey estimate is solid enough to publish.

The estimates for elevated blood pressure:

Group: Kids surveyed; Estimate; Range it could plausibly be.
Non-Hispanic white: Kids surveyed: 460; Estimate: 0.5%; Range it could plausibly be: 0.1% – 1.6%.
Non-Hispanic Black: Kids surveyed: 447; Estimate: 2.0%; Range it could plausibly be: 0.3% – 6.4%.
Non-Hispanic Asian: Kids surveyed: 164; Estimate: 0.9%; Range it could plausibly be: 0.0% – 5.1%.
Hispanic: Kids surveyed: 589; Estimate: 2.5%; Range it could plausibly be: 1.4% – 4.1%.

Elevated blood pressure is rare in children — roughly 1 in 50 or fewer in every group. But rare outcomes are exactly the ones that are hardest to measure: only a handful of kids in each sample actually had it, so the estimates wobble.

## The point being illustrated

NCHS judges reliability two ways, and the example is built to show that they disagree:

The old way (relative standard error). Measure the error as a share of the estimate itself. When the estimate is tiny, almost any error looks huge in relative terms. The white estimate has an RSE of 58% — well past the 30% cutoff — so this rule would have thrown it out, even though the estimate is pinned down to a range barely 1.5 percentage points wide. That's the flaw: it punishes an estimate for being small, not for being imprecise.

The current way (confidence interval width). Ask instead how wide the plausible range is, in actual percentage points:

- Narrow range → publish. White (1.6 points) and Hispanic (2.7 points) are both tight enough to be useful. Both get published.
- Wider range → look closer. Black (6.1 points) and Asian (5.1 points) are wide enough to warrant a second check — is the range wide compared to the estimate? For Black children, the range is 3 times the size of the estimate; for Asian children, more than 5 times. Both blow past the 130% limit, so both are suppressed. "2.0%" and "0.9%" aren't reported, because the data can't distinguish them from "nearly zero" or "several times higher."

confidence interval of 2.7.

Other checks all passed for every group: each had at least one child with elevated blood pressure but not all of them, and each had enough degrees of freedom (more than 8) for the statistics to behave.

## The mirror-image wrinkle

Every row has a flip side: the share with normal or borderline blood pressure (99.5%, 98.0%, 99.1%, 97.5%). These carry exactly the same uncertainty — the range for Black children is still 6.1 percentage points wide — but now that width sits next to a number near 100 instead of near 2. As a fraction of the estimate it's about 6%, comfortably under the limit.

So the same underlying data gets published one way and suppressed the other. NCHS handles this honestly rather than quietly: the "normal or borderline" figures are printed with a footnote saying their complement didn't meet the standard. Readers who want to subtract from 100 to recover the suppressed number are warned that the number wasn't trustworthy enough to print.

## The takeaway

A percentage on its own says nothing about whether it can be trusted. Small samples, split into subgroups, measuring a rare condition, produce numbers that look specific but aren't. These rules decide what gets published, what gets flagged, and what gets withheld — and the white-children row is the whole argument in miniature: under the old rule it vanishes, under the current one it's perfectly publishable.

## Plain-language version

What this is: NCHS's rulebook (from the Data Presentation Standards for Proportions, Parker et al., Vital and Health Statistics Series 2, No. 175) for deciding whether a percentage calculated from survey data is solid enough to publish, or too shaky and should be withheld. Each estimate has to clear a series of checks.

Check 1 — Is the group big enough?
A percentage has to be based on at least 30 people (and, for surveys with complex sampling designs, at least 30 in the "effective" sample size too, which accounts for the design). Fewer than 30 in either sense, and the estimate isn't published.

Special case: if nobody in the group had the outcome (0%) or everybody did (100%), the group size itself is used to build the margin of error. Such an estimate isn't automatically published — even if it passes everything else, a statistical reviewer looks at it and decides whether it goes out or gets withheld.

Check 2 — How wide is the margin of error?
For groups that pass Check 1, analysts compute a 95% confidence interval — the range the true value is likely to fall in — using the Clopper-Pearson method, or Korn-Graubard for complex surveys. The width of that range drives everything that follows.

- Very narrow (up to 5 percentage points): publishable, as long as at least one person had the outcome and the estimate passes the degrees-of-freedom check (a separate test of whether the survey design supports a reliable interval). If it's a 0% or 100% estimate, or it fails the degrees-of-freedom check, it goes to a reviewer for a judgment call.
- Very wide (30 percentage points or more): too imprecise. Not published.
- In between (5 to 30 points): one more test — see Check 3.

Check 3 — Is the margin of error large compared with the estimate itself?
A 10-point margin means something very different around an estimate of 60% than around one of 5%. So the width is expressed as a percentage of the estimate (the "relative" width).

- More than 130% of the estimate: the uncertainty swamps the number. Not published.
- 130% or less: publishable, provided the degrees-of-freedom check passes.

The underlying idea: a number is only released when readers can trust it to mean something. ## What this section is saying, in plain language

The basic problem. NCHS publishes rates — deaths per 100,000 people, births per 1,000 women, doctor visits per 100 people. A rate is just a numerator (the number of events) divided by a denominator (the population those events could have happened to). When either number is small or shaky, the resulting rate can bounce around a lot for no meaningful reason. So the agency has long used rules of thumb to decide when a rate is too unreliable to publish.

The old vital statistics rule: 20 events. For births and deaths recorded in the National Vital Statistics System, the rule was simple — don't publish a rate built on fewer than 20 events. The reasoning: counts of events like deaths behave like a Poisson process, meaning their standard error is just the square root of the count. At 20 events, that works out to a relative standard error (RSE) of about 23% — roughly, the noise is a quarter the size of the estimate. So "fewer than 20 events" and "RSE of 23% or more" were two ways of describing the same cutoff. Age-adjusted death rates followed the same rule.

When the denominator itself is an estimate. Usually the denominator is a population count from the decennial census, or a postcensal/intercensal estimate built from it. Those are treated as essentially fixed — any random wobble in them is small enough to ignore. But for some groups — specific Hispanic subpopulations, or breakdowns by education level — the population figure doesn't come from the census. It comes from a survey like the American Community Survey or the Current Population Survey, which means it carries its own sampling error. In those cases, the uncertainty in the denominator has to be folded into the calculation, and reliability was judged by the RSE of the rate directly (again, 23% or more got suppressed or flagged for review).

The health care surveys used a different rule: "30/30." Nearly all survey-based rates at NCHS come from the National Health Care Surveys — mostly rates of visits to hospitals and providers. Here the numerator is estimated from a sample rather than counted from a register, while the denominator is typically still a census-based population figure. The convention was: suppress the rate if it rested on fewer than 30 sampled observations, and flag it as unreliable if the RSE exceeded 30%. Those two conditions together were known as the 30/30 rule, and the same standard applied to published counts, not just rates.

Where the noise comes from. Two distinct sources. Sampling variability arises whenever a number is estimated from a sample — you surveyed some people, not all of them, and a different sample would have given a somewhat different answer. Natural (stochastic) variability exists even when nothing is sampled: the actual number of deaths in a county last year is a complete count, but it's still one realization of an underlying random process, and it could have come out differently. Vital statistics counts are complete but are still modeled as Poisson for this reason. Census-based population denominators, by contrast, have variability so small it's set aside.

A subtlety about sample size. In complex surveys with clustering and stratification, the raw ("nominal") number of respondents overstates how much information you actually have. The effective sample size — the size of a simple random sample that would give equal precision — is the more meaningful figure, because it reflects the survey's design and therefore its real statistical power. Separately, survey estimates are weighted up to represent the whole population, so the weighted estimate of events or population is a much larger number than the count of people actually interviewed. Reliability decisions are based on the nominal and effective sample sizes, never on those inflated weighted figures.

One gap. Cases where both the numerator and the denominator came from surveys were rare, so there was no standing rule — those were handled one at a time as they came up.

## Plain-language version

In 2016, the UK's private education industry brought in around £42.6 billion in total turnover.

That figure comes from a survey, not a full count of every business, so it carries some uncertainty. Statisticians measure that uncertainty with a "confidence interval" — a range around the estimate that reflects how much the number might shift if a different sample had been surveyed.

For this estimate, the range runs from about £41.6 billion to £43.7 billion (the estimate give or take roughly £1.0 billion).

What that range means: if you repeated the survey 20 times, drawing a fresh random sample each time, and worked out a range like this for each one, about 19 of those 20 ranges would contain the true figure for the whole industry, and about 1 would miss it. So a range built this way is a reliable — though not guaranteed — guide to where the true number sits.

## One correction to flag

The original's final sentence — "there is a 95% chance that the true population value lies between £41,616 million and £43,682 million" — is the standard misreading of a confidence interval, and it contradicts the sentence just before it.

The 95% describes the method, not this particular interval. The true value is a fixed (if unknown) number; it either falls inside this specific range or it doesn't. What's random is which interval the sampling procedure produced. Saying "95% chance the true value is in this range" is a Bayesian credible-interval statement, which requires a prior and is not what was calculated here.

I dropped that sentence from the restatement rather than reproducing it. If you want the intuition it was reaching for, the honest general-audience phrasing is: "we can be 95% confident the true figure lies in this range," where "confident" points at the track record of the method.

## Plain-language version

In 2016, the UK's private education industry brought in around £42.6 billion in total turnover.

That figure comes from a survey, not a full count of every business, so it carries some uncertainty. Statisticians measure that uncertainty with a "confidence interval" — a range around the estimate that reflects how much the number might shift if a different sample had been surveyed.

For this estimate, the range runs from about £41.6 billion to £43.7 billion (the estimate give or take roughly £1.0 billion).

What that range means: if you repeated the survey 20 times, drawing a fresh random sample each time, and worked out a range like this for each one, about 19 of those 20 ranges would contain the true figure for the whole industry, and about 1 would miss it. So a range built this way is a reliable — though not guaranteed — guide to where the true number sits.

## One correction to flag

The original's final sentence — "there is a 95% chance that the true population value lies between £41,616 million and £43,682 million" — is the standard misreading of a confidence interval, and it contradicts the sentence just before it.

The 95% describes the method, not this particular interval. The true value is a fixed (if unknown) number; it either falls inside this specific range or it doesn't. What's random is which interval the sampling procedure produced. Saying "95% chance the true value is in this range" is a Bayesian credible-interval statement, which requires a prior and is not what was calculated here.

I dropped that sentence from the restatement rather than reproducing it. If you want the intuition it was reaching for, the honest general-audience phrasing is: "we can be 95% confident the true figure lies in this range," where "confident" points at the track record of the method.

Comparing how reliable two survey estimates are

Surveys don't measure everything — they sample. So every survey figure comes with a margin of uncertainty, called the standard error, which says roughly how much the estimate might wobble if you'd surveyed a different sample.

Two examples from 2016:

- UK plastering businesses turned over an estimated £2,322 million, give or take about £201 million.
- An estimated 155,000 people worked full-time in agriculture, forestry and fishing, give or take about 12,400.

Those two "give or take" figures look nothing alike — £201 million versus 12,400 people. But they're measured in different units, so comparing them directly is meaningless.

The fix is to express each margin as a percentage of the estimate it belongs to. That percentage is called the coefficient of variation:

- £201 million ÷ £2,322 million = 0.087, or 8.7%
coefficient of variation of 8.7%.
- 12,400 ÷ 155,000 = 0.08, or 8%

coefficient of variation of 8.7%.
coefficient of variation of 8%.

Once put on the same scale, the two are nearly identical. Both estimates are about equally precise — each carries roughly 8% uncertainty relative to its own size — even though one deals in millions of pounds and the other in thousands of people.

Industry: Total turnover (£ millions); Standard error (£ millions); Relative standard error.

Water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation: Total turnover (£ millions): £34,677 million; Standard error (£ millions): £222.7 million; Relative standard error: 0.01 (1%).

In plain terms

These numbers come from a survey rather than a count of every business, so each total is an estimate. The extra columns say how precise that estimate is.

- Private education providers took in about £42.6 billion in 2016.
- Water, sewerage and waste companies took in about £34.7 billion.

The standard error is the typical amount an estimate like this would wobble by if the survey were run again with a different sample of businesses — roughly £527 million for education and £223 million for water and waste. The relative standard error simply expresses that wobble as a share of the total. For both industries it is about 1%, meaning the estimates are considered reliable: the true figure is very likely close to the number shown.

Under the previous NCHS guidance, vital rates whose denominators came from surveys (CPS or ACS) — where sampling variability had to be accounted for — were assessed on the RSE of the rate itself, and rates with an RSE of 23% or greater were suppressed or flagged for internal review.

That 23% threshold is the survey-denominator analogue of the 20-event rule: for a Poisson count, SE = √n, so 20 events gives RSE = √20/20 ≈ 22.4% ≈ 23%. Age-adjusted death rates followed the same pair of criteria — presented if based on 20+ events, or if from survey-estimated populations with RSE under 23%.

Note this is distinct from the National Health Care Surveys' "30/30 rule" (suppress under 30 sample observations, flag if RSE > 30%).

Under the previous ("30/30 rule") guidance for the National Health Care Surveys, the minimum was 30 sample observations in the numerator:

- Fewer than 30 sample observations → suppressed (not published at all).
- 30 or more → publishable, but flagged as unreliable if the RSE exceeded 30%.

Two notes from the passage worth keeping straight:

- The 30 refers to nominal sample observations, not the sample-weighted estimate of events. For complex surveys, nominal and effective sample sizes — not the weighted counts — determine reliability.
- The same 30/30 criteria applied to counts as well as rates: counts were suppressed below 30 sample observations and flagged when RSE > 30%.

This is distinct from the NVSS side, where the threshold was 20 events in the numerator (corresponding to a 23% RSE under a Poisson assumption) for rates with census/postcensal/intercensal denominators.

One caveat on the passage's wording: the first interpretation given ("if we drew 20 random samples… 19 out of 20 would contain the true value") is the correct frequentist reading, but the closing sentence — "there is a 95% chance that the true population value lies between £41,616 million and £43,682 million" — is the standard misinterpretation. Under frequentist inference the population value is fixed, not random; the 95% describes the long-run coverage of the procedure, not the probability that this particular interval contains the value. That interval either contains it or it doesn't. (The probabilistic reading is only valid for a Bayesian credible interval.) The two sentences in the source contradict each other; the first is the one to keep.
